Let’s talk about something we all encounter on the meditation path— imperfection. Chapter 7 is called: The Ongoing Nature of Practice: Embracing Imperfection.
No matter how long you’ve been practicing, there are always days when your mind feels wild, your heart heavy, or your body just...restless. That whole idea of perfect meditation—endless calm, unbroken focus—it honestly doesn’t last. What we’re left with is something much more real: practice that’s ongoing, and a path where imperfection isn’t just possible—it’s expected.
Picture someone who’s been meditating for years. Maybe it’s even you. And still, every now and then, those old habits pop up—snapping at someone you love, worrying about what’s next, feeling overwhelmed by life’s daily noise. That wave of discouragement hits. Maybe there’s a sense of failure. But then, maybe a memory surfaces—a teacher’s words, or just the gentle nudge of a friend. “Begin again,” that voice whispers. So, you take a slow breath. You come back to your practice, letting go of all that self-judgment.
Most folks don’t realize—meditation isn’t about locking in some permanent state of peace. It’s really about coming back, over and over, to right here, right now. Every time your mind wanders, every time frustration creeps in, there’s a chance to practice patience and kindness for yourself. Think about it: the real growth? It happens in those moments when you’re willing to start again, not when everything feels perfectly still.
There’s a story that captures this. After a rough week, someone sits down to meditate. Their mind is racing—worries, plans, judgments, all swirling around. But instead of fighting the thoughts, they just notice them. Maybe they silently name each one: “planning,” “remembering,” “judging.” And then, gently, they return to the breath. The thoughts don’t vanish, but the grip loosens. There’s more space inside. It’s a reminder—thoughts are just thoughts. They aren’t facts.
Embracing imperfection means letting go of that urge to be a “good” meditator. It’s about accepting that some days will be easier than others, and setbacks? They’re just part of the journey. Over time, this gentle acceptance starts to spill out into the rest of your life. Mistakes become opportunities for understanding, not for shame. Difficult emotions are allowed to be there, instead of being pushed down. Relationships—even with yourself—become more forgiving.
The ongoing nature of practice is both humbling and, honestly, pretty freeing. There’s no finish line to cross, no ultimate destination. Instead, there’s a lifelong process of learning, growing, and returning. Every moment is a new chance to begin again. To meet yourself with compassion. And to trust—right here, right now—that the path is always unfolding.
